Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Making any plans for the future

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette: The blast that tore through the downtown market still lives in Malik’s bones. He remembers the sudden vacuum of air, the deafening crack, and the suffocating smoke that coated his tongue. His colleagues were gone in an instant, dragged under rubble that had been solid moments before. That chaotic suffocation and the unpredictable violence are why the smell of burnt rubber now locks his chest, and why the sudden clatter of a dropped fabric bolt in his tailor shop feels like another detonation. In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle. There were entire stretches of the aftermath he simply could not remember, no matter how hard he pressed his fingers to his temples. When fragments did surface, they played on a relentless loop, vivid and unyielding. Yet, his lingering conviction that he was fundamentally weak and that he belonged nowhere actively shaped how those memories surfaced; because he believed he had failed to protect himself and his community, his mind began to fracture the trauma into emotionless, detached recollections, as if he were merely an observer of a stranger’s tragedy. The replaying footage itself also wired his nervous system into a permanent state of alert. Within months, Malik found himself scanning every doorway the moment he stepped into a space, his eyes darting to fire escapes and side doors before he even reached the counter. He refused to sit facing the floor, pressing his spine firmly against the interior wall so he could watch the street. The constant need to monitor the perimeter left him exhausted, but the relief of having an unobstructed view was the only thing that kept the panic at bay. Those corrosive beliefs and the relentless alertness soon dictated how he survived each day. Because he no longer trusted his own judgment to keep himself safe, Malik began avoiding any conversation that looked toward the horizon, convinced that preparing for tomorrow was pointless. The exhausting hypervigilance of scanning exits and pressing his back to the wall left him with no emotional bandwidth, so he gravitated toward his phone, scrolling through games and videos for hours to keep his mind occupied. The strategy worked until the isolation bred resentment, and he would deliberately pick fights with delivery drivers or customers, manufacturing drama to outrun the quiet. When the shop grew quiet and the intrusive memories threatened to surface, that same self-doubt pushed him toward these distractions. Yet the unrelenting threat monitoring only fed his original convictions; the more he scanned for danger and found it everywhere, the more certain he became that he belonged nowhere, and that he was fundamentally inadequate. He stopped making plans for the year ahead, convinced that the future could be erased in a single breath. The tension between his hyperawareness of the present and his conviction that he was fundamentally broken only intensified; the more he scanned for danger, the more his memories replayed, and the more he felt his own fragility, driving him back to his screens and his arguments, tightening the loop that kept him trapped. Now, at thirty-three, the exhaustion has finally eclipsed the numbness. The recent loss of a long-term client, who cited his erratic behavior and withdrawn nature as the reason for taking his work elsewhere, pushed Malik to the edge. He walked into the clinic today hoping someone might finally help him untangle the noise in his head. He is terrified that the help will come too late to save his livelihood, but he holds onto the faint hope that he might learn to trust himself again.
